name: English Learners With Disabilities
title: English Learners With Disabilities
answer: Some English learners also have disabilities, and separating a language difference from a disability is one of the hardest judgments in education. AI cannot make that distinction and must never be used to suggest one. Once a student has an IEP, language and disability services must be planned together, with the family included in their own language.

sections.body: This idea addresses the overlap between learning English and having a disability, a situation where the two can look alike and are genuinely difficult to tell apart. A student who struggles to read might be learning English, might have a learning disability, or might have both, so evaluations have to be designed to separate language from disability, often by testing in the student's home language. The problem is that a wrong call in either direction harms the student, whether by missing a disability or by mislabeling a language learner. AI tools cannot make this distinction, and the text is explicit that they should never be used to suggest one. The idea also covers what happens after identification, when language and disability services must work together rather than in separate tracks.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the work begins with evaluation that deliberately separates language from disability, often using testing in the student's home language. Once a student has an IEP, the English language development specialist and the special education team plan jointly rather than separately. The accessibility tools described in Chapter 12 and the language supports in this chapter can often be combined, and the IEP team decides how that combination works. The family takes part in these decisions in their own language. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports one finding: poor interpretation has been found to reduce these families' access to special education services and their trust in schools (Tang Yan, 2022). Beyond that citation, the text offers no study or figure on the distinction between language and disability itself, so the core claim that AI cannot make this distinction rests on practice and professional judgment rather than on research presented here.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are stated plainly. AI tools cannot distinguish language learning from disability and should never be used to suggest one, so that judgment stays with qualified people. A qualified human interpreter should be present at every IEP meeting for a family that needs one, because machine translation is not good enough for decisions this important. The IEP team, not a tool, decides how accessibility and language supports are combined. Families of English learners with disabilities face double barriers, and poor interpretation has been linked to reduced access to services and reduced trust in schools, which is why the human interpreter requirement is treated as a safeguard rather than a convenience.
